name: The Cathari (Albigensian) heresy and its persecution
plain_explanation: The Cathari, strongest in southern France (where they were called Albigenses), were dualists who believed matter itself was evil, created by a wicked demiurge (identified with the Old Testament God), and that only the New Testament revealed the true, good God. They rejected the resurrection of the body, practiced strict asceticism (vegetarianism excepting fish, rejection of marriage) for an elite class of 'the perfected,' while ordinary adherents lived more normal lives. Innocent III called a Crusade against them in 1209, conducted with great ferocity, and the movement was ultimately stamped out through war and, from 1233, the newly founded Inquisition.
precise_definition: A dualist heretical movement, descended via the Bogomiles of Bulgaria from the Paulicians and ultimately Manichaeanism, holding that matter is evil and that the created world is the work of a wicked demiurge distinct from the true, good God revealed in the New Testament.
why_it_mattered: Its scale and popularity (including among southern French nobility) exposed how widely the wealth and moral corruption of the clergy had alienated ordinary believers, motivating the Church's crackdown via Crusade and the institutional invention of the Inquisition.
historical_origin: Traced by Russell from Marcion (ca. 150 AD) and the Gnostics, through the Paulicians (an Armenian sect) and the Bogomiles of Bulgaria, reaching Italy and southern France via contact during the Crusades; a Bulgarian delegation attended a Cathari council near Toulouse in 1167.
examples: Cathari vegetarianism, with an exception for fish (believed not to be sexually generated)
The Cathari view that marriage is worse than adultery because it is 'continuous and complacent'
The distinction between the ordinary faithful and the 'perfected,' who alone were held to strict precepts
objections: Russell cautions that Cathari doctrine is known 'with certainty' only through hostile testimony, and that persecutors, being versed in the history of heresy, tended to attribute the tenets of older sects to new ones on the basis of loose resemblance
competing_positions: Orthodox Catholic doctrine, which affirmed the goodness of the created material world and the resurrection of the body
influence_on_later_thinkers: The Albigensian Crusade (1209) and the 1233 founding of the Inquisition by Gregory IX to combat this and related heresies established institutional and legal machinery (denial of counsel after 1254, confiscation of property, handover to the 'secular arm') that persisted for centuries and was later used, for instance, against Joan of Arc.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Many southern French nobles supported the Cathari partly for the opportunity to seize Church lands, illustrating how religious dissent and material/political interest were intertwined.
